title: A riddle without the answer
short: The snake is never named: the poem works as a riddle, describing the creature only through glimpses and effects.
body: Dickinson often writes riddle-poems that withhold their subject (compare 'I like to see it lap the Miles', on a train). Here the snake is a 'narrow fellow', a social term that treats it like a slightly suspect acquaintance. When the poem was printed without her consent in the Springfield Daily Republican on 14 February 1866, the editors titled it 'The Snake', and the 1891 Poems (Second Series) kept the title, supplying the answer she had left out. The archive text is that of the 1891 edition, which differs from her manuscripts in several words (see 'when a child' and 'at morn').

title: rides
short: The snake 'rides' through the grass as if mounted, a surprising verb for a creature without legs.
body: The verb suggests ease and speed, as if the snake were a rider passing through, and it continues the comic social register of 'fellow'. It may also hint at the gliding, wave-like motion of a snake's body, which seems carried rather than walking. 'Occasionally' makes the encounter a matter of chance, preparing for the suddenness stressed in l. 4. The verb is the first of several that make the snake human and sociable.

title: 'did you not / His notice sudden is'
short: Dickinson complained that the Republican's question mark spoiled the sense; ll. 3-4 were meant to run together.
body: In early 1866 Dickinson wrote to T. W. Higginson that her snake had been 'robbed of me' and 'defeated too of the third line by the punctuation. The third and fourth were one'. Her manuscript reads 'You may have met Him - did you not / His notice sudden is': that is, 'did you not notice him? His notice is sudden', or 'if you did not, it is because his appearance is so sudden'. The newspaper's question mark after 'not' cut the syntax in two. The archive's 1891 text, with a comma after 'him', keeps something of her run-on. Johnson's note records that a copy sent to Susan Dickinson around 1872 reads 'instant' for 'sudden'.

title: The grass divides as with a comb
short: The snake's path parts the grass like a comb parting hair; then the grass closes and opens further on.
body: The simile is domestic and exact: the grass parts in a line, briefly revealing 'a spotted shaft', and closes behind. We see the movement, not the animal. The 'shaft' (a spear-shaft or arrow) gives the snake the straightness of a weapon, and 'spotted' recalls the markings of an American garter or milk snake. The stanza's quiet present tense makes the encounter feel recurrent and close ('at your feet').

title: a boggy acre, a floor too cool for corn
short: The snake likes damp, marshy ground too cold for growing corn (maize): useless land, outside cultivation.
body: 'Acre' is a farmer's measure, and 'floor' a domestic word, so the snake's habitat is described in the terms of a household and a farm. Corn (in American usage maize) needs warm soil; the boggy acre is a wild margin that human cultivation leaves alone. The lines quietly separate the snake's world from the human one before the speaker's memory brings them together.

title: 'when a child' (manuscript: 'when a Boy')
short: Dickinson wrote 'when a Boy'; the 1891 editors changed it to 'child', removing her male speaker.
body: Both Dickinson's manuscript copies read 'when a Boy, and Barefoot', and 'at Noon' rather than 'at morn' in the next line; the 1891 editors, Mabel Loomis Todd and T. W. Higginson, altered both words, presumably to make the speaker match the woman poet. Dickinson often used male or child personae (she told Higginson in 1862 that the speaker of her verse was 'a supposed person', not herself), and the boy's barefoot rambles suit the scene. Modern editions (Johnson 1955, Franklin 1998) restore 'Boy'. The archive text keeps the 1891 reading, so students should be aware of the variant.

title: a whip-lash unbraiding in the sun
short: The child mistakes the snake for a whip-lash lying in the sun; when he stoops to pick it up, it wrinkles and is gone.
body: A whip-lash is the braided leather thong of a whip. 'Unbraiding' is the poem's finest word: it suggests both the loosening coils of the snake and a braided thing coming undone, as if the object had come alive. The child's mistake turns the snake from a tool into a living creature in an instant, and 'wrinkled' catches the ripple of its sudden movement. The dangerous whip is also a hint of the snake's menace, preparing the fear of the last stanza.

title: Several of nature's people
short: The speaker is on friendly terms with most creatures, feeling for them 'a transport of cordiality'.
body: 'Nature's people' treats animals as neighbours, continuing the social language of 'fellow'. 'Transport', in Webster's 1844 dictionary (which Dickinson used), means rapture or ecstasy, and 'cordiality' comes from Latin cor, heart: a warm, heartfelt friendliness. The Latinate, slightly formal phrasing is playful, as if the speaker were describing social calls, and it sets up the sharp contrast with the visceral last stanza.

title: Attended or alone
short: Whether in company or by oneself, the encounter with the snake always produces fear.
body: 'Attended' (accompanied, waited on) keeps the courtly, social idiom of the poem: the speaker could meet the snake with companions or alone, and it would make no difference. The line widens the experience from the single childhood memory to every meeting since. 'Attended' may also suggest a lady or gentleman with servants in attendance, so that the snake meets the speaker as one social being meets another; whatever the company, the body reacts the same way, as the final two lines record. The courtly word thus sets up the abrupt shift into physical fear.

title: 'a tighter breathing / And zero at the bone'
short: The closing image of fear: a catch of breath and an absolute cold felt in the bones.
body: The end is one of Dickinson's most quoted images. 'Tighter breathing' is the physical shock of fear; 'zero at the bone' gives it a temperature, as if the body's marrow fell to zero degrees, the lowest number and freezing point. The abstract mathematical word set against the bodily 'bone' is typical of her compression. Critics also hear the old association of the serpent with the Fall (Genesis 3), so that the speaker's instinctive horror carries a trace of an ancient enmity: 'I will put enmity between thee and the woman' (Genesis 3:15). The poem's light social comedy thus gives way to a fear no friendliness can tame.

anchor: A floor too cool for corn
title: Metre: common measure varied
short: Quatrains in alternating lines of four and three stresses, Dickinson's hymn metre, with slant rhymes.
body: The poem uses the common metre of English hymnody (as in Isaac Watts), with lines of eight and six syllables alternating, rhymed on the second and fourth lines; in the third stanza the first line is shortened ('He likes a boggy acre'). Many rhymes are slant ('seen' / 'on', 'sun' / 'gone'), some are full ('alone' / 'bone'), and 'me' / 'cordiality' rhymes on a lightly stressed final syllable. The run-on from stanza three to four ('at morn, // Have passed') imitates the long, surprised memory.
